item.title: Iran warns citizens against travel to France, Belgium and Italy amid violent unrest
item.description:
Iran warns citizens against travel to France, Belgium and Italy amid violent unrest

Submitted by Elis Gjevori on Tue, 10/20/2026 - 11:04
Tehran challenges Paris over protester rights as French police face scrutiny over serious injuries to students
A fire burns and destroys the city hall in the French city of Limoges on 17 October after a group of forced entry into the building during ongoing protests (AFP/Pascal Lachenaud)
Off

The Iranian foreign ministry has advised its citizens to avoid non-essential travel to France, Belgium and Italy following the “intensification of unrest and disruption of public order” in those countries.

The ministry issued the advisory on Monday as France faced increasingly violent protests driven partly by a cost-of-living crisis worsened by the Israeli-US war on Iran.

“Compatriots currently in France, Belgium and Italy are advised to avoid being in tense areas and conflict zones and to avoid unnecessary travel, especially in unstable areas,” the Iranian foreign ministry said.

At least two people have died during the protests in France, while police have arrested at least 2,000 people.

Reports of serious injuries among protesters include two who lost their hands to stun grenades.

Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi condemned French President Emmanuel Macron on X for siding with US President Donald Trump in the war against Iran.

“Macron made his bed when he assured POTUS that he welcomes atrocities against Iranians,” said Araghchi on Monday.

“Too late to blame the war his ilk helped cause. The French people demand wholesale change, including freedom of assembly. Listen to the future of France, Mr President,” added Araghchi.

Authorities in French cities have also banned protests, while the government has refused to rule out a state of emergency that would expand police powers to conduct searches and make arrests.

Amnesty International has condemned French police for using unnecessary and disproportionate force against the mainly student protesters.

The president of Amnesty International France, Anne Savinel-Barras, said: “Children and young people peacefully demanding their right to education must be protected rather than being beaten, tear-gassed, or arbitrarily detained.”

'No one listens to us': France's mass student protests expose social and racial inequality
Read More »

In the Paris suburbs, police fired a tear-gas projectile into the face of a 14-year-old boy named Eden, breaking his jaw and smashing his teeth, Reuters reported.

Tehran’s rebuke challenges the credibility of a government that has supported protests in Iran while cracking down on demonstrations at home.

On 6 October, Iranian foreign ministry spokesman Esmaeil Baghaei accused France of double standards over its condemnation of repression in Iran during mass street protests earlier this year.

“In January 2026, France spoke of the need to respect 'peaceful assembly without fear of punishment' in Iran, and to exercise “restraint” on the part of the government towards protesters,” said Baghaei, arguing that Paris had taken that position despite “incitment to riots” in Iran.

“In France, student protests are now being called 'urban violence.' The interior minister is not very supportive of restraint, calling for swift and decisive intervention by security forces and the use of force to restore order,” noted Baghaei.

“Why are the same behaviors and the same standards interpreted one way when the protester is in Iran and another way when the protester is in France?!” he added.

Thousands of people were reported to have been killed in a brutal crackdown by Iranian authorities following mass street protests in January, with security forces opening fire on crowds with live fire and arresting thousands. 

At the time, Amnesty International said: “Even by the Iranian authorities’ own bleak record of committing gross human rights violations and crimes under international law during successive waves of protests, the severity and scale of killings and repression since 8 January is unprecedented.”

On 7 October, French Foreign Minister Jean-Noel Barrot summoned Iran’s ambassador to France over what Paris described as a “disinformation campaign carried out by the Iranian authorities regarding the high school student movement in France”.

item.title: Badenoch says Tories would prioritise cutting taxes for businesses over individuals – UK politics live
item.description:
Conservative leader also called for benefit spending to be cut to fund rise in defence budget

Badenoch says Britain needs tax cuts.

We need to get out of the way of job creators who make our country richer. We need to encourage risk taking, wealth creation, enterprise.

Britain’s tax burden has never been higher. You are taxed on the heating in your home. You’re taxed at the petrol pump filling up your car. You’re taxed when you insure that car. You’re taxed if you take the family away on holiday. You’re taxed if you stay in the UK thanks to Andy Burnham’s tourist tax. You’re taxed to buy a home, taxed to live in a home, taxed to pass on your home. This is clearly not working. Britain does not feel better off.

Andy Burnham wrote in The Times yesterday about the moral outrage of the current benefit system. But as far as I could work out, his answer is to spend even more on benefits.

item.description:
Turkey's parliament set to ratify Mecca Joint Defence Agreement

item.title: Pakistan army chief arrives in Tehran to meet senior officials
item.description:
Pakistan army chief arrives in Tehran to meet senior officials

Pakistan army chief Field Marshal Asim Munir arrived in Tehran on Tuesday with a delegation of Pakistani officials to meet senior Iranian officials, according to Iran’s semi-official Mehr news agency.

The visit comes against the backdrop of a diplomatic stalemate between Tehran and Washington, with the reopening of the strategic Strait of Hormuz a key sticking point.

item.title: IRGC says two tankers hit mines, set ablaze south of Hormuz
item.description:
IRGC says two tankers hit mines, set ablaze south of Hormuz

Two tankers were set ablaze and brought to a halt south of the Strait of Hormuz after hitting Iranian mines, the Revolutionary Guards' Navy said in a statement shared by state media on Tuesday, without saying when the tankers were hit.

The statement also said a US drone was downed by Iran on Monday night.

Reporting by Reuters

item.title: Ex-Greens co-leader urges council groups to reject Zionism policy
item.description:
Exclusive: Adrian Ramsay calls conference motion a distraction and says councillors should maintain coalitions where possible

  • UK politics live – latest updates

Adrian Ramsay, the former co-leader of the Greens, has urged his party’s councillors to reject the newly adopted “Zionism is racism” motion if it will help them stay in power in local government, in a fresh sign of internal dissent over the policy.

Ramsay, one of the Greens’ five MPs, said he was pleased that a number of Green council groups had already condemned the policy, which was adopted at the party’s conference and also calls for a single Palestinian state in place of Israel.

item.title: Healey to reject calls to raise capital gains tax in budget
item.description:
Cabinet colleagues have previously called for an increase but chancellor feels it might ultimately cost the Treasury

  • UK politics live – latest updates

John Healey will not raise capital gains tax in next week’s budget, despite previous calls to do so from cabinet colleagues including Louise Haigh and Wes Streeting.

The chancellor has decided that any increase might ultimately cost the Treasury if wealthy individuals defer the sale of assets or move them out of the country, according to Treasury sources.

item.title: Myanmar’s ousted leader Aung San Suu Kyi seen in rare photos after receiving gift from King Charles
item.description:
Critics said images of detained former leader were a stunt by the military to end country’s diplomatic isolation

Myanmar has delivered presents from Britain’s ​King Charles to Aung San Suu Kyi, releasing rare photos of the imprisoned former leader in what critics said was a stunt by the country’s military to end diplomatic isolation.

A presidential spokesperson said on social media that home ministry officials handed over two gardening books on soil, “along with one sealed envelope and a sealed diplomatic pouch”, from King Charles, who is known to have an interest in planting and the environment.
